name: Solange Delery
languages: French (convent-school French, which opens doors on Esplanade Avenue)
equipment: Heavy overcoat, a man's camel-hair coat, cut down for her by a tailor who owed her a favor; the lining has two pockets the tailor did not mention
Derringer (Remington over-and-under), 2 rounds loaded, in a garter holster or the coat lining depending on the dress
Switchblade, pearl-handled, in her evening bag
Evening clothes: a green silk gown, gloves to the elbow and a paste necklace that photographs like emeralds
Good suit, for daytime and lawyers
Business cards (100) for three different names: Mlle. Solange Delery, Mrs. Laura Fenwick of Natchez, and Miss Noelie Ory, secretary
Cigarette case (silver plate) with an engraving from a man she will not name
A fifth of rye, half full
An IOU for $2,000 signed L. Ste. C. on a napkin from the Oneiros club rooms on Carondelet Street
features: Knows the Block (City-Born origin, New Orleans: quickest way across any neighbourhood, which bars and clubs belong to whom; advantage on Streetwise checks to find a person, place or service in the city)

The Long Con (Grifter: in downtime she can build a cover identity in a day for $20; she can keep two; while in a prepared cover she has advantage on Deception, Performance and Persuasion to keep it up, and casual checks against it succeed without a roll. Her two covers are Mrs. Laura Fenwick of Natchez, a widow with cotton money, and Miss Noelie Ory, a secretary from the Carnival committee)

Cheap Shot (Grifter: once per turn, +2d6 damage to one creature she hits with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm if she has advantage, if another enemy of the target is within 5 ft of it, or if the target believed a lie she told it in the last minute)
Quick Hands (Grifter, 2nd level: a bonus action each turn to Dash, Disengage, Hide or make one Sleight of Hand check)
Racket: Roper (Grifter, 3rd level: a person she has talked to for 10 minutes treats her as a friend until given a reason not to, and will do a favor that costs them nothing without a check)

Back Door of Every Club (Nightclub Singer background: she can walk in the stage door of any club in town, and bartenders, cigarette girls, waiters and musicians tell her who was there last night, who they sat with and who paid)

personality.traits: I sing like I mean it and lie like I mean it, and I am never quite sure which one I am doing. I remember every name and every drink order. I tip big when I am broke so no one knows I am broke.
personality.ideals: Every one of those men on Esplanade Avenue was given everything and still cheats at cards. I was given nothing and I have never once cheated anyone who could not afford it.
personality.bonds: The Café Isabeau, its band and its bartender, Ulysse, who are the nearest thing I have to family. My sister Honorine in Mobile and her two boys, whom I send money every month. And, God help me, a man named Lucien Ste. Claire, who owes me two thousand dollars and once, for about six weeks, made me believe him.
personality.flaws: I cannot resist a mark who thinks he is smarter than me. I drink a little more than I sing. And I have told so many people so many stories that I sometimes cannot find my own.

appearance: A tall, fine-boned woman of twenty-nine with a long neck, auburn hair worn in a roll, green eyes and a beauty mark she draws on when she is someone else. She dresses a step above her money, in a man's camel coat over whatever she sang in last night, and moves like a woman who has walked out of a lot of rooms without hurrying.
backstory: Solange Delery was born above a bakery on Burgundy Street in the French Quarter, the daughter of a pastry cook and a Sicilian seamstress, and was taught at the Ursuline convent school by nuns who despaired of her and gave her the voice lessons anyway. At sixteen she was singing in the lounge of a Canal Street hotel; at twenty she was the canary at the Café Isabeau on Bourbon Street, a small, smoky, respectable-enough club where old-line Carnival men bring women who are not their wives. She learned that the men of the krewes will tell a singer anything, because they do not think of her as a person, and she learned to sell what they told her, carefully, to men who would pay. In the winter of 1945 she fell, briefly and badly, for Lucien Ste. Claire, the president of a shipyard and, everybody whispers, the secret captain of the Krewe of Oneiros, who was charming, unhappy and broke, and who borrowed two thousand dollars from her in January 'until the sale goes through'. On Thursday night, 28 February, he came into the Isabeau at half past eleven white as paper and drank four double ryes without speaking, and on Friday morning she read that one of his clerks was dead in the canal. She would like her money back. She would also, she finds, like to know.
